sections.h2: Are solar panels worth it in the UK in 2026?
sections.answer: **For most homes, yes.** A typical 4 kW system costs £5,000 to £7,000 and pays for itself in about 11 to 12 years on our figures, then keeps working for 25 years or more. Your export tariff and how much you use at home matter more than where you live.

sections.h2: What a solar system really costs in 2026
sections.title: What does a solar system really cost?
sections.answer: **£5,000 to £7,000 for a typical 4 kW system**, with no VAT until 31 March 2027. The government's figures put the median at £1,546 to £1,595 per kW.

sections.h2: How much electricity will your roof generate?
sections.answer: **About 3,444 to 4,036 kWh a year from a 4 kW system** on a clean south facing roof, depending on the city. Manchester makes about 13% less than London; Cardiff slightly more.

sections.h2: How roof direction and pitch change output
sections.title: Does roof direction and pitch matter?
sections.answer: **South is best, but east and west still make about 80%**, and a shallow north facing roof about two thirds. Pitch barely matters on a south facing roof.

sections.h2: Solar panel output by month in the UK
sections.title: How much do solar panels generate each month?
sections.answer: **About two thirds of the year's output comes from April to September.** July makes about 3.4 times what December does in London, so no battery carries you through winter.

sections.h2: How many solar panels do you need?
sections.answer: **Most homes need about 7 to 12 panels.** A medium user of 2,500 kWh a year needs about 2.6 kWp to generate what they use in a year, though most of that use will still come from the grid.

sections.h2: How much of your solar will you actually use?
sections.answer: **Usually less than a quarter without a battery.** A typical 4 kW system on a medium use home uses 14% to 23% of its output, rising to about half with a 5 kWh battery.

sections.h2: Is a solar battery worth it?
sections.answer: **Not on solar alone.** A 5 kWh battery costs about £4,600 and adds about £178 a year in a typical home, so it takes about 26 years to pay back and lasts 10 to 12. A time of use tariff, an electric car or a heat pump can change that.

sections.h2: Smart Export Guarantee rates in September 2026
sections.answer: **From 4.1p to 17.5p per kWh**, depending on the tariff. Outgoing Octopus pays 12p to Octopus customers; the highest rates are tied to buying your system from that supplier.

sections.h2: Worked example: a 4 kW system in Birmingham
sections.answer: **Payback from 8.3 to 19.2 years on the same roof**, depending only on the export tariff: 10.8 years on Outgoing Octopus at 12p.

sections.h2: How long do solar panels take to pay for themselves?
sections.answer: **About 11 to 12 years**: 10.7 years in the south to 12.3 in Scotland on our figures, and much longer on a 4p export tariff. The panels then keep producing for 25 years or more.

sections.h2: What a Victorian terrace heat pump really costs
sections.answer: **About £12,200 to £12,700 installed, or £4,700 to £5,200 after the £7,500 grant.** A terrace sits near the national median of £12,908 because solid walls, sashes and bare floors lose a lot of heat.

**£12,700 at the median for an unimproved terrace, or £5,200 after the £7,500 grant.** Most jobs pay £3,500 to £8,000 after the grant, with radiators and the pipe run to the cylinder setting the price.

sections.h2: Victorian terrace versus semi versus modern terrace
sections.answer: **About the same as a 3-bed semi to install, at £12,700.** Unimproved it costs £55 a year more than the semi to run on a heat pump tariff; insulating the walls turns that round.

sections.h2: What size heat pump, and insulate first in cost order
sections.answer: **7 to 9 kW, depending on insulation.** Start with the loft at about £750 and draught-proofing at around £250; internal wall insulation, around £12,000, takes the unit from 8 kW to 7 kW.

sections.h2: Which heat pumps suit a Victorian terrace
sections.answer: **Models with high flow temperatures, such as the Vaillant aroTHERM plus and Mitsubishi Ecodan R290 at 75°C.** They let the installer design at 55°C and keep more radiators; pre-1919 homes did no worse in the government trial.

sections.h2: Cast iron radiators, cylinder and pipework
sections.answer: **Cast iron radiators can stay if they are big enough, and many are.** Expect a few to change; pipework is where terrace quotes vary most, with primaries running 10 to 20 metres to the cylinder.
**£760 a year on a heat pump tariff, £107 less than gas.** On a standard tariff it costs £1,010, £143 more than gas; insulating the walls to band C cuts the tariff bill to £487.

sections.h2: The Boiler Upgrade Scheme for a terrace
sections.answer: **£7,500 off the quoted price, bringing the heat pump to £4,700 to £5,200.** It is £9,000 until March 2027 for oil or LPG homes with no mains gas, and you no longer need a valid EPC.

sections.h2: Is a heat pump worth it for a Victorian terrace
sections.answer: **Only just, on a heat pump tariff: about £1,700 more than a gas boiler, paid back in about 16 years at £107 a year.** On a standard tariff it never pays back, costing £143 a year more than gas.

sections.h2: Placement, conservation areas and two party walls
sections.answer: **In the rear yard, usually on the side wall of the outrigger.** It must pass the MCS 020(a) sound test at both neighbours' windows; a conservation area does not stop it, but a listed terrace needs planning permission.

**Get three quotes from MCS-certified installers and compare the design, not the price.** Each should include a heat loss calculation using the real solid wall figure, the design flow temperature, a radiator schedule and a sound calculation.

**Installed prices come from DESNZ Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics**, efficiency from the Electrification of Heat trial, energy prices from the Ofgem price cap and insulation costs from the Energy Saving Trust.

sections.h2: What a 5-bed heat pump really costs in 2026
sections.answer: **£14,000 to £19,500 installed for a typical 5-bed, or £6,500 to £12,000 after the £7,500 grant.** Price data for the very largest single units is thin, so treat those costs as less certain.
**£14,000 to £19,500 for the whole job, median £16,100.** After the £7,500 grant most households pay £6,500 to £12,000, or £5,000 to £10,500 with the £9,000 grant for oil or LPG homes.
**The biggest step on the ladder: £14,000 to £19,500 for a 5-bed against £12,500 to £18,000 for a 4-bed.** The extra £1,400 at the median takes about 18 years to earn back on a heat pump tariff.

sections.h2: What size heat pump for a 5-bed house
sections.answer: **Around 13.5 to 17.5 kW, typically 16 kW, sometimes as two units in cascade.** Insulating an average house to well insulated drops it to 13.5 kW and saves about £700 on the median installation.

sections.h2: Which heat pumps suit a 5-bed house
sections.answer: **Large single units such as the Daikin Altherma 3 H HT at 14 kW, 16 kW and 18 kW, or two smaller units in cascade.** Your electrical supply, single or three phase, narrows the choice before brand does.
**Expect 6 to 9 of the 14 to 18 radiators to be upsized, plus a larger cylinder.** Set guest rooms back a couple of degrees rather than off, because closing them off makes the heat pump cycle.
**£1,250 a year on a heat pump tariff, £304 less than gas.** On standard electricity it costs £1,662, £108 more than gas, so the tariff decides whether it adds up.

sections.h2: The Boiler Upgrade Scheme for a 5-bed
sections.answer: **£7,500, or £9,000 for oil or LPG homes until 31 March 2027, whatever the size of the house.** On a 5-bed that covers only 38% to 54% of the job, and a cascade gets one grant, not two.

sections.h2: Is a heat pump worth it for a 5-bed house
sections.answer: **Only on a heat pump tariff, and slowly: a payback of about 8 to 26 years at £304 a year.** On standard electricity it never pays back; against oil it saves £1,083 a year.

sections.h2: Electrical supply, DNO approval and cascades
sections.answer: **On a 5-bed the supply becomes a real question.** Above 60 amps of maximum demand the installer must apply to the network operator before fitting, and two single phase units in cascade can sometimes avoid a three phase unit.

**Get three quotes from installers who have fitted 14 kW and larger systems, and compare the design.** Each should cover the heat loss, one unit or a cascade, the electrical survey and DNO route, and every radiator.
**Installed costs come from DESNZ Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics**, efficiency from the Electrification of Heat trial, energy prices from the Ofgem price cap and the oil price from BoilerJuice.

sections.h2: What a 3-bed detached heat pump really costs
sections.answer: **£11,000 to £15,500 installed for a typical 3-bed detached, or £3,500 to £8,000 after the £7,500 grant.** It needs about 9.5 kW, and insulation moves the range from £10,500 to £16,500.
**£11,000 to £15,500 for the whole job, median £13,000.** After the £7,500 grant most pay £3,500 to £8,000, or £2,000 to £6,500 with the £9,000 grant; radiators decide where you land.
**Between a 3-bed semi and a 4-bed detached, and close to the semi.** The fourth exposed wall adds about £300 to the median installation; the jump to a 4-bed detached is the bigger one.

sections.h2: What size heat pump for a 3-bed detached house
sections.answer: **Around 8 to 10.5 kW, typically 9.5 kW.** Insulating a typical house to well insulated drops it to 8 kW and takes about £600 off the median installed cost.

sections.h2: Which heat pumps suit a 3-bed detached house
sections.answer: **Any major brand's unit in the 8 to 12 kW class; at this size the design matters more than the brand.** R290 units such as the Vaillant aroTHERM plus reach 75°C and can keep more existing radiators.

**Expect 4 to 6 of the 10 to 12 radiators to be upsized, plus a new cylinder.** Microbore pipework, common from the 1970s, is the usual budget breaker and often needs replacing with 15mm or 22mm pipe.

sections.h2: Running costs: 3-bed detached on gas and oil
sections.answer: **£750 a year on a heat pump tariff, £182 less than gas and £650 less than oil.** On a standard tariff it costs £997, £65 more than gas, but still beats oil by £403.
**£7,500, or £9,000 for oil or LPG homes with no mains gas until 31 March 2027.** That leaves £3,500 to £8,000 to pay on gas, or £2,000 to £6,500 on oil or LPG.

sections.h2: Is a heat pump worth it for a 3-bed detached house
sections.answer: **On gas, only on a heat pump tariff.** At £182 a year the payback runs from immediately to about 25 years. Against oil the case is clear, saving £650 a year.

sections.h2: Placement, noise and planning on a detached plot
sections.answer: **Placement is where a detached house wins.** With a side and rear wall to choose from and neighbours further away, the sound calculation is easier to pass, and planning permission is not normally needed.

**Get three MCS quotes and compare the design, not the headline price.** Check the heat loss calculation, a flow temperature of 50°C or lower, the radiator schedule, the grant rate and, on oil, who removes the tank.
**Installed costs come from DESNZ Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics**, efficiency from the Electrification of Heat trial, energy prices from the Ofgem price cap and the oil price from BoilerJuice.

sections.h2: What a 2-bed terrace heat pump really costs
sections.answer: **£10,000 to £14,000 installed, or £2,500 to £6,500 after the £7,500 grant.** Fixed costs such as the cylinder, survey and commissioning mean a small terrace costs only a little less than a 3-bed semi.
**£10,000 to £14,000 for the whole job, median £11,700.** After the £7,500 grant most pay £2,500 to £6,500; a new cylinder and a cupboard for it are what separate a terrace from a semi.
**About the same as a 2-bed flat, and less than an end-terrace.** A mid-terrace costs £10,000 to £14,000 against £10,500 to £15,000 for an end-terrace and £11,000 to £15,500 for a 3-bed semi.

sections.h2: What size heat pump for a 2-bed terrace
sections.answer: **Around 5 to 6.5 kW, typically 5.5 kW.** That is the small end of most ranges; insulating first also lifts efficiency, which matters more to the running cost than the kWh saved.

sections.h2: Which heat pumps suit a small terrace
sections.answer: **Small units from every major brand, such as the Vaillant aroTHERM plus at 3.5 kW or 5 kW.** For a terrace, choose on depth, sound power and flow temperature, and get a sound calculation for the exact yard spot.

**Two or three of the five to seven radiators usually need upsizing.** The bigger problem is finding room for a cylinder in a combi-heated terrace, and microbore runs often need replacing with 15mm pipe.
**£449 a year on a heat pump tariff, £109 less than gas.** On standard electricity it costs £596, £38 more than gas; a well insulated terrace beats gas on either tariff.

sections.h2: The Boiler Upgrade Scheme for a terrace
sections.answer: **£7,500 off the invoice, leaving £2,500 to £6,500 to pay.** It covers roughly half to three quarters of the job, and a terrace qualifies like any other house you own.

sections.h2: Is a heat pump worth it for a 2-bed terrace
sections.answer: **Only on a heat pump tariff: at £109 a year the payback runs from immediately to about 30 years.** A terrace with generous radiators and an airing cupboard pays back fastest; a standard tariff gives no saving.

sections.h2: Noise, the rear yard and two party walls
sections.answer: **In the rear yard, where it must pass the MCS 020(a) sound calculation at both neighbours' windows.** Avoid tight corners, which score worse; a fence or wall between unit and window often gets a terrace through.

**Get three MCS quotes and compare the design, not the headline price.** Check the heat loss calculation, the radiator schedule, where the cylinder goes with the cupboard priced, and a sound calculation for both neighbours.

**Installed costs come from DESNZ Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics**, efficiency from the Electrification of Heat trial, energy prices from the Ofgem price cap and insulation costs from the Energy Saving Trust.

sections.h2: What a 3-bed semi heat pump really costs
sections.answer: **A typical 3-bed semi costs £11,000 to £15,500 installed, or £3,500 to £8,000 after the £7,500 grant.** That is for a 9 kW heat pump; a well insulated semi needs 7.5 kW and a poorly insulated one 10 kW.
**The whole job is £11,000 to £15,500, median £12,700, or £3,500 to £8,000 after the grant.** Radiators are what most often push a quote outside that range, so ask whether radiator work is included.
**All three cost the same, £11,000 to £15,500 installed, because each needs a heat pump in the 8 to 10 kW band.** One shared wall saves only about 630 kWh of heat a year against a detached house.

sections.h2: What size heat pump for a 3-bed semi
sections.answer: **Most 3-bed semis need around 7.5 to 10 kW, with a typical semi at 9 kW.** The installer's room-by-room heat loss calculation sets the real size, and insulating first can bring it down to 7.5 kW.

sections.h2: Which heat pumps suit a semi
sections.answer: **Every major manufacturer makes a unit in the 7 to 10 kW class, and at this size the brands are close.** Ask for a design flow temperature of 50°C or lower and a sound calculation for the outdoor unit.

**Expect to upsize some of the 8 to 10 radiators, fit a heat pump cylinder and possibly replace microbore pipe.** The cylinder is in the recorded job cost; ask the installer to check pipe sizes at the survey.
**A heat pump costs £705 a year on a heat pump tariff, £172 less than gas, but £937 on standard electricity.** That is £60 a year more than the £877 gas bill, so the tariff decides the economics.

sections.h2: The Boiler Upgrade Scheme for a semi
sections.answer: **The grant is £7,500, or £9,000 for oil or LPG homes off the gas grid until 31 March 2027.** It takes a typical semi to £3,500 to £8,000, and the installer deducts it from the invoice.

sections.h2: Is a heat pump worth it for a 3-bed semi
sections.answer: **On gas, only with a heat pump tariff.** A £172 a year saving pays back the extra over a new boiler in anything from immediately to about 26 years. Against oil it saves about £611 a year.

sections.h2: Noise, placement and the party wall
sections.answer: **Site the outdoor unit away from the party wall so it passes the 37 dB limit at the neighbour's nearest window.** Most semis pass without extra work, and planning permission is not normally needed.

**Get three MCS quotes and compare the design, not the headline price.** Each should include a room-by-room heat loss calculation, a radiator schedule, a sound calculation and the £7,500 or £9,000 grant deducted.

**Costs come from the DESNZ Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics, August 2026.** Efficiency comes from the Electrification of Heat trial, prices from the Ofgem price cap and BoilerJuice, and heat demand from our NEED-based model.

sections.h2: What a 4-bed heat pump really costs in 2026
sections.answer: **A typical 4-bed detached costs about £14,700 installed, with most jobs £12,500 to £18,000 before the grant.** It needs about 12 kW, so it sits in the upper half of all air source jobs.
**The whole job is £12,500 to £18,000, median £14,700, or £5,000 to £10,500 after the £7,500 grant.** Radiators are what most often move a quote outside that range.
**A 4-bed semi costs about the same, £13,000 to £18,000 installed, because it uses slightly more heat.** It needs 12.5 kW against 12 kW for a detached, so do not budget on the semi being cheaper.

sections.h2: What size heat pump for a 4-bed house
sections.answer: **A typical 4-bed detached needs about 12 kW, from 10 kW well insulated to 13.5 kW poorly insulated.** The installer's room-by-room heat loss calculation sets the real size.

sections.h2: Which heat pumps suit a 4-bed house
sections.answer: **Every major manufacturer makes units at 10 to 16 kW, and brand matters less than design.** Ask for a design flow temperature of 50°C or lower and the seasonal performance the installer expects in the quote.
**Expect 4 to 7 of the 10 to 14 radiators to need upsizing, plus a heat pump cylinder.** The cylinder is in the recorded job cost; microbore pipework is the common budget breaker on long runs.
**A heat pump costs £936 a year on a heat pump tariff, £228 less than gas, but £1,244 on standard electricity.** That is £80 a year more than gas, so the tariff decides the economics.

sections.h2: The Boiler Upgrade Scheme for a 4-bed
sections.answer: **A 4-bed gets the same £7,500 grant, or £9,000 for oil or LPG homes off the gas grid until 31 March 2027.** There is no limit on house value, and the installer deducts it from the invoice.

sections.h2: Is a heat pump worth it for a 4-bed house
sections.answer: **On mains gas it is a weak case.** At £228 a year on a heat pump tariff, the extra over a new boiler takes about 5 to 29 years to earn back. Against oil it saves £811 a year.

sections.h2: Ground source vs air source for a 4-bed
sections.answer: **Air source is the practical choice at £12,500 to £18,000, against £18,000 to £42,000 for ground source.** Ground source suits a detached house with plenty of land and a long ownership horizon.

**Get three MCS quotes and compare the design, not the headline price.** Each should include a heat loss calculation, a radiator schedule, a sound calculation and the £7,500 or £9,000 grant deducted from the invoice.

**Costs come from the DESNZ Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics, August 2026.** Efficiency comes from the Electrification of Heat trial, prices from the Ofgem price cap and BoilerJuice, and heat demand from our NEED-based model.

sections.h2: Why old houses need extra preparation
sections.answer: **Old houses lose heat faster, so the heat pump must run hotter unless you insulate.** Yet in the government trial pre-1919 homes did as well as newer ones, at 2.90 units of heat per unit of electricity.
**Do the loft first, then solid walls, draught-proofing and windows.** A loft top-up costs about £600; internal wall insulation costs around £12,000 but cut gas use by a median 17.3%.

sections.h2: Choosing the right heat pump for an old house
sections.answer: **Air source, sized by a room-by-room heat loss survey.** Once insulated, old houses need from 5 kW for a 2-bed terrace to 10 kW for a 4-bed detached, at medians of £11,500 to £13,300.

sections.h2: Radiator upgrades: do you need them?
sections.answer: **Probably, but not always, because a heat pump runs at 35 to 45 degrees instead of 55 to 70.** Large original cast iron radiators can often stay, and upgrades done in the job are part of the installed price.

sections.h2: Cost breakdown for a typical old house
sections.answer: **A solid-walled 3-bed Edwardian semi costs around £18,000 in total after the grant.** That is the £12,700 median heat pump job less £7,500, plus internal wall insulation, a loft top-up and draught-proofing.

sections.h2: Running costs: heat pump vs gas boiler in an old house
sections.answer: **On a heat pump tariff it costs £705 a year against £877 for gas, but £937 on standard electricity.** The tariff saving is £172 a year for a 3-bed Edwardian semi.
**Most old houses need no planning permission, but listed buildings always do.** Conservation areas limit units facing a road, and every unit must meet the 37 dB noise limit at a neighbour's window.

sections.h2: Common concerns with heat pumps in old houses
sections.answer: **A correctly designed heat pump keeps an old house warm and does not damage the walls.** You will need a hot water cylinder, and the original airing cupboard can often take it.

sections.h2: Step-by-step: getting a heat pump in your old house
sections.answer: **Insulate first, then get three MCS quotes with a full heat loss calculation.** The installer claims the £7,500 grant, or £9,000 for oil or LPG homes, and installation takes a few days.

**Costs come from the DESNZ Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics, August 2026.** Efficiency comes from the Electrification of Heat trial, insulation costs from the Energy Saving Trust and prices from the Ofgem price cap.
**Installed costs run from £10,000 to £14,500 for a 1 to 2 bed flat to £14,000 to £19,500 for a 5 bed detached.** The £7,500 grant comes off every one.

sections.h2: What is included in the installed cost?
sections.answer: **The heat pump, cylinder, controls, pipework, labour and VAT are all included.** Radiator and pipework upgrades often are but not always, so ask whether they are in your quote.
**Size follows the house: 4.5 to 6 kW for a flat, 9 kW for a 3-bed semi and about 16 kW for a 5-bed detached.** A typical semi pays £3,500 to £8,000 after the grant.
**Going from poorly to well insulated takes a 3-bed semi from 10 kW to 7.5 kW.** It cuts the heat pump tariff bill from £853 to £546 a year, a fall of 36%.

sections.h2: Ground source vs air source by house type
sections.answer: **Air source is the practical choice for most homes.** The middle half of ground source jobs cost £18,136 to £42,110, and it only suits larger detached homes with enough land.

sections.h2: The BUS grant and total out-of-pocket cost
sections.answer: **The £7,500 grant, or £9,000 for oil or LPG homes until 31 March 2027, brings a 3-bed semi to £3,500 to £8,000.** It comes off the installer's invoice; Scotland has a separate scheme.
**A heat pump saves only on a heat pump tariff: £705 a year for a 3-bed semi against £877 on gas.** On a standard tariff every house type is £38 to £108 a year worse off.

**Costs come from the DESNZ Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics, August 2026.** Efficiency comes from the Electrification of Heat trial, prices from the Ofgem price cap and insulation data from the Energy Saving Trust and NEED.

sections.h2: What a 1960s house heat pump really costs
sections.answer: **About £12,700 installed for a typical 1960s semi, or £5,200 after the £7,500 grant.** Filled cavities bring the median to £12,300 and unfilled ones push it to £13,300.

sections.h2: The cavity wall is the whole story
sections.answer: **Filling an empty cavity roughly halves the wall's heat loss, for around £2,200.** Band E to band C takes the heat pump from 10 kW to 7.5 kW and £307 a year off a tariff bill.
**About £5,200 after the £7,500 grant, from a £12,700 median installation.** The middle half pay £3,500 to £8,000 after the grant, so ask what each quote leaves out.

**The 1960s house reaches band C for a fraction of the cost.** Cavity fill costs around £2,200 against around £12,000 for internal wall insulation on a Victorian terrace, leaving £4,800 and £4,700 after the grant.
**Big windows, thin lofts, mixed floors, draughts and microbore pipework turn up on most surveys.** A loft top-up to 270mm costs about £600; ask the installer to check pipe sizes at the survey.

sections.h2: What size heat pump for a 1960s house
sections.answer: **About 9 kW for a typical 1960s semi, 10 kW with open cavities and 7.5 kW once they are filled.** The installer's room-by-room calculation decides, so check the wall U-value it used.

sections.h2: Which heat pumps suit a 1960s house
sections.answer: **Any of the main 7 to 10 kW units can do it; the design decides the result.** Ask for a flow temperature of 50°C or lower, expected performance in writing and an MCS 020(a) sound calculation.

**A 1960s semi usually needs fewer radiator changes than a Victorian terrace, and they sit inside the installed price.** The old airing cupboard often takes the new cylinder, and a whole re-plumb is rarely needed.
**£705 a year on a heat pump tariff against £877 for gas, but £937 on standard electricity.** Filling the cavities to reach band C cuts the tariff bill to £546.

sections.h2: Why a leaky house is the worse case, not the better one
sections.answer: **The worse the house, the smaller the saving.** On a heat pump tariff the band E house saves £120 a year against gas and the band C house £199, so fill the cavity first.

sections.h2: The Boiler Upgrade Scheme for a 1960s house
sections.answer: **The grant is £7,500 for almost every 1960s house, because they are on mains gas.** Oil or LPG homes with no gas get £9,000 until March 2027, and open cavities no longer block the grant.

sections.h2: Is a heat pump worth it for a 1960s house
sections.answer: **Only on a heat pump tariff.** The £5,200 after the grant is about £1,700 more than a new boiler and pays back in about 10 years at £172 a year; on standard electricity there is no payback.

sections.h2: Noise, placement and the estate layout
sections.answer: **Most 1960s plots pass the noise test easily because the houses are spaced wider apart.** The MCS 020(a) calculation must show 37 dB or less at the neighbour's nearest window, and planning permission is not normally needed.

**Get three MCS quotes and compare the design, not the headline price.** Each should show the wall U-value used, how the cavity was checked, the flow temperature, a radiator schedule and a sound calculation.

**Our heating model built on DESNZ NEED data, DESNZ Boiler Upgrade Scheme prices and the Electrification of Heat trial.** Energy prices come from the Ofgem price cap and insulation costs from the Energy Saving Trust.

sections.h2: What an end terrace heat pump really costs
sections.answer: **About £12,600 installed for a typical 3-bed end terrace, or £5,100 after the £7,500 grant.** Insulation moves the median from £12,200 well insulated to £13,000 with a bare solid gable.
**About £5,100 after the £7,500 grant, from a £12,600 median job.** The middle half pay £3,500 to £8,000; radiators, cylinder and pipework decide where you land, not the heat pump.

sections.h2: End terrace versus mid terrace versus semi
sections.answer: **Almost exactly midway between a mid terrace and a semi.** It uses 9,270 kWh against 8,820 kWh and 9,900 kWh, and costs £660 a year on a heat pump tariff against £628 and £705.

sections.h2: The gable wall, and what it actually costs
sections.answer: **About £40 a year on gas in the typical case, which is not much.** Its construction sets the range: going from poorly to well insulated saves £287 a year on a heat pump tariff and £800 off the installation.

sections.h2: What size heat pump for a 3-bed end terrace
sections.answer: **About 8.5 kW for a typical 3-bed end terrace, 7 kW well insulated and 9.5 kW with a bare solid gable.** Check the U-value the installer's heat loss calculation gives the gable.

sections.h2: Which heat pumps suit an end terrace
sections.answer: **Any of the main 7 to 9 kW units can do it; the design decides the result, not the badge.** Ask for a flow temperature of 50°C or lower, expected performance in writing and an MCS 020(a) sound calculation.

**Several radiators usually need upsizing, starting with the rooms against the gable, and that work is part of the installed price.** A surviving airing cupboard usually takes the cylinder; check for microbore at the survey.
**£660 a year on a heat pump tariff, £161 less than gas, but £878 on standard electricity.** On a standard tariff the heat pump costs £57 a year more than the gas boiler.

sections.h2: Insulation changes the answer more than size does
sections.answer: **A worse insulated end terrace saves less, not more.** On a heat pump tariff the saving against gas falls from £186 well insulated to £161 typical and £112 poorly insulated.

sections.h2: The Boiler Upgrade Scheme for an end terrace
sections.answer: **The grant is £7,500, or £9,000 for oil or LPG homes with no mains gas until March 2027.** The installer takes it off the quote, and a well-insulated end terrace then pays £4,700.

sections.h2: Is a heat pump worth it for an end terrace
sections.answer: **Only on a heat pump tariff.** A typical end terrace pays £5,100 after the grant, about £1,600 more than a new boiler, which £161 a year pays back in about 10 years.

sections.h2: Placement, the side wall and one neighbour
sections.answer: **Easier than a mid terrace: one attached neighbour, and a gable facing none of their windows.** A unit near the gable usually passes the 37 dB MCS 020(a) test without an acoustic enclosure.

**Get three MCS quotes and compare the design, not the headline price.** Each should state the gable's wall construction and U-value, the flow temperature, a radiator schedule and a sound calculation.
**DESNZ NEED 2026 data for heat demand, DESNZ Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics for prices and the Electrification of Heat trial for efficiency.** Energy prices come from the Ofgem price cap.

sections.h2: Two beds or three: which guide you need
sections.answer: **Use this page for a bungalow of roughly 70 square metres; larger ones fit the main bungalow guide.** The 2-bed median job is about £700 cheaper and £147 a year cheaper to run on a heat pump tariff.

sections.h2: What a 2-bed bungalow heat pump really costs
sections.answer: **£10,500 to £15,000 for a typical 2-bed bungalow, or £3,000 to £7,500 after the £7,500 grant.** Insulation barely moves the price: only £600 separates the best and worst insulated medians.
**The typical job is £10,500 to £15,000, median £12,300, and £3,000 to £7,500 after the grant.** Oil or LPG homes pay £1,500 to £6,000; radiator upgrades and microbore can add to it.
**It costs more to heat than any other two bedroom home except a detached house.** A 2-bed bungalow uses 31% more heat than a 2-bed mid terrace and 23% more than a 2-bed semi.

sections.h2: Why one storey costs more to heat
sections.answer: **Spreading out doubles the roof and floor.** A 2-bed bungalow has about 222 square metres of heat losing envelope against about 185 for a two storey house, so the loft and floor matter as much as the walls.

sections.h2: What size heat pump for a 2-bed bungalow
sections.answer: **About 7.5 kW for a typical 2-bed bungalow, 6.5 kW well insulated and 8.5 kW poorly insulated.** Top up the loft, about £600, before the survey so the installer sizes to the improved house.

sections.h2: Loft insulation is the biggest lever here
sections.answer: **The loft is about a third of the heat losing envelope, and cheap to fix.** Going from average to well insulated saves £133 a year on a heat pump tariff, with the loft the cheapest part.

sections.h2: The floor is the second largest surface
sections.answer: **The ground floor is the second largest heat losing surface and rarely gets insulated.** A suspended timber floor with a crawl space is the easy case; a solid concrete floor is rarely worth doing alone.

sections.h2: Which heat pumps suit a 2-bed bungalow
sections.answer: **Any of the main 6 to 9 kW units can do it; the design decides the result.** Ask for a flow temperature of 50°C or lower, expected performance in writing and an MCS 020(a) sound calculation.
**Usually 2 to 3 of the 5 to 7 radiators need upsizing, and short single floor pipe runs keep the job simple.** The cylinder needs a cupboard of at least 80cm by 80cm, not the loft.
**£590 a year on a heat pump tariff against £733 on gas, but £784 on standard electricity.** Off the gas grid it saves £511 a year against oil on a heat pump tariff.
**£7,500 from the Boiler Upgrade Scheme, or £9,000 for oil or LPG homes with no mains gas until 31 March 2027.** That brings the whole job to £1,500 to £6,000 off the gas grid.

sections.h2: Is a heat pump worth it for a 2-bed bungalow
sections.answer: **On mains gas the case is thin; off the gas grid it is strong.** On gas, payback at £143 a year runs from immediate to about 30 years, while against oil the saving is £511 a year.

**The unit must pass the MCS 020(a) test of 37 dB at a neighbour's nearest window, which is harder on an attached bungalow.** Keep controls simple: one thermostat, weather compensation and a steady low flow temperature.

**Get three MCS quotes and compare the design, not the price.** Check the loft depth assumed, the unit size against the heat loss, the radiator schedule, the cylinder cupboard and, off gas, the £9,000 grant rate.

**DESNZ Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics for prices, our heat model built on DESNZ NEED 2026 and the Electrification of Heat trial for efficiency.** Energy prices come from Ofgem and oil prices from BoilerJuice.

sections.h2: What a bungalow heat pump really costs
sections.answer: **About £12,300 to £13,000 installed for a typical 2 or 3 bed bungalow, or £4,800 to £5,500 after the £7,500 grant.** Oil or LPG bungalows with no mains gas take a further £1,500 off.
**A 3 bed bungalow pays about £5,500 after the £7,500 grant, from a £13,000 median.** With the £9,000 oil or LPG grant it is £4,000; ask what each quote excludes, such as oil tank removal.
**A 3-bed bungalow sits next to a 3-bed detached house, not a smaller one.** It needs 9.5 kW and costs £13,000 installed, because its roof and floor are each as large as its floor area.

sections.h2: What size heat pump for a bungalow
sections.answer: **About 7.5 kW for a 2 bed bungalow and 9.5 kW for a 3 bed.** Top up the loft, about £600, before the survey, though on its own it rarely changes the heat pump size.

sections.h2: Which heat pumps suit a bungalow
sections.answer: **Any of the main 7 to 10 kW units can do it; the design decides the result.** Ask for a flow temperature of 50°C or lower, expected performance in writing and an MCS 020(a) sound calculation.

sections.h2: Radiators, cylinder and pipework on one floor
sections.answer: **A few radiators usually need upsizing, and short single floor pipe runs make the job quicker.** With no landing, the cylinder needs a cupboard of at least 80 cm by 80 cm, not the loft.
**£737 a year on a heat pump tariff, £180 less than gas and £639 less than oil.** On standard electricity it costs £980, which is £63 more than gas.

**Oil or LPG bungalows with no mains gas get £9,000 until March 2027.** That takes a typical 3 bed bungalow from £13,000 to £4,000, and low income households may get the work free through the council.

sections.h2: Is a heat pump worth it for a bungalow
sections.answer: **On gas only with a heat pump tariff; on oil, clearly yes.** On gas £180 a year pays back the extra £2,000 in about 11 years; on oil £4,000 at £639 a year pays back in about six.
**Site the unit away from the party wall, because bungalow windows sit at unit height.** It must pass the 37 dB MCS 020(a) test; ask for quiet mode at night and a single zone set to 20°C.
**Get three MCS quotes and compare the design, not the price.** In a bungalow check the loft depth assumed, the radiator schedule, where the cylinder goes and, for oil or LPG, the £9,000 grant rate.

**DESNZ Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics for prices, our heating model built on DESNZ NEED data and the Electrification of Heat trial for efficiency.** Energy prices come from Ofgem and oil prices from BoilerJuice.

sections.h2: Current rules: what landlords must do
sections.answer: **Band E is the legal minimum to let.** Properties rated F or G cannot be let unless an exemption is registered, and fines reach a maximum of £5,000 per property.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to improve your EPC?
sections.answer: **About £1,200 is often enough to move from F to E.** That covers loft insulation, heating controls and LED lighting; reaching C usually needs wall insulation or a heating upgrade, with spending capped at £10,000 under the 2030 rules.

sections.h2: Cheapest upgrades to reach Band E
sections.answer: **Start with loft insulation, then cavity walls, heating controls, LEDs and draught-proofing.** An F home needs between 1 and 18 more points to reach E at 39, and a bare loft costs about £750 to insulate.

sections.h2: Preparing for a minimum of C
sections.answer: **Every privately rented home must meet a band C equivalent standard by 1 October 2030.** Landlords must spend up to £10,000 per property including VAT, and the maximum fine rises to £30,000 per property per breach.

**Register an exemption if E is out of reach.** Exemptions last 5 years; the cost cap exemption applies when the remaining improvements would cost more than £3,500 including VAT, rising to £10,000 under the 2030 rules.

**Some, but fewer than owner-occupiers get.** The £7,500 Boiler Upgrade Scheme grant applies when replacing fossil fuel heating, 0% VAT applies to rental homes, and ECO4 can help if the tenant gets a qualifying benefit.

**Improvement costs can be offset for tax.** Like-for-like replacements such as a new boiler are allowable expenses in the year, while new capital improvements such as insulation or solar count against Capital Gains Tax on sale.
**A better rating helps letting because tenants notice bills.** The median band E home costs about £479 a year more to run than the median band C home at October 2026 prices.
**£55 to £150, and usually under an hour.** A typical two or three bedroom house costs £65 to £95; give the assessor loft access and invoices for any improvements to get the best rating.

**Rules and penalties come from GOV.UK and the government response of 21 January 2026**, costs from the Energy Saving Trust and DESNZ, band shares from the English Housing Survey and running costs from DESNZ NEED.

sections.h2: Heat pump vs gas boiler running costs by property type
sections.answer: **The tariff decides it.** A 3 bed semi costs £877 a year with gas, £937 with a heat pump on a standard tariff and £705 on a 19.8p heat pump tariff.
**Divide heat demand by the COP, then multiply by the electricity price.** At 26.32p and a COP of 2.78, heat costs 9.5p per kWh against 8.9p for gas, or 7.1p on a heat pump tariff.

sections.h2: What is COP and why it matters
sections.answer: **COP is heat out per unit of electricity in, so higher means cheaper.** The median trial home got 2.78 over a year, giving heat at 9.5p per kWh on a standard tariff against 8.9p for gas.

sections.h2: How to reduce your heat pump running costs
sections.answer: **Switch to a heat pump tariff first.** Cosy Octopus works out at about 19.8p per kWh against the 26.32p cap rate; then insulate, run at low flow temperatures and hold a steady temperature.

sections.h2: Heat pumps vs oil and LPG
sections.answer: **A heat pump is cheaper even on a standard tariff.** It cuts the cost of heat by about 29% against oil and 15% against LPG, or 46% and 36% on a heat pump tariff.

**Check the efficiency your system reports over a season.** Below about 2.5 puts it in the bottom quarter of trial homes, so ask your installer to check flow temperature, refrigerant charge and radiator sizing.

**Prices come from the Ofgem price cap for October to December 2026**, efficiency from the Electrification of Heat trial, oil from BoilerJuice, the tariff from Cosy Octopus and heat demand and insulation savings from DESNZ NEED.

sections.h2: Before you start: is DIY right for your loft?
sections.answer: **Yes, if the loft is easy to reach, dry and has visible joists.** Call a professional for damp, a flat roof, a converted room, suspected asbestos or lots of wiring, and check for free ECO4 insulation first.

**100mm rolls between the joists and 170mm rolls across them, to reach 270mm.** Add eaves trays, pipe lagging, a tank jacket, hatch insulation and safety kit: an FFP2 or FFP3 mask, goggles and gloves.

**Clear the loft, fit eaves trays, lay 100mm between the joists, then 170mm across them.** Lag pipes, jacket the tank sides and top, keep cables on top and never lay boards directly on the insulation.

**The worst mistake is blocking eaves ventilation, which causes condensation and rot.** Also avoid compressing the wool, leaving gaps, insulating under the tank, burying cables and covering downlights without fire-rated caps.
**DIY costs only materials.** A professional charges about £600 to top up from 120mm or £750 from nothing, and a grant can make it free if you are eligible.

sections.h2: Savings and payback by property type
sections.answer: **The measured saving is modest, a median 3.2% less gas.** That is £28 a year for a 3 bed semi, a 21 year payback on a £600 professional top-up; DIY pays back sooner.
**Next, draught-proof, look at wall insulation and then your heating.** Insulating first means a new heat pump or boiler is sized correctly, and a new EPC will show the improvement.

**Suitability, depth and cost come from the Energy Saving Trust**, measured savings from the DESNZ NEED Impact of Measures report and energy prices from the Ofgem price cap for October to December 2026.
**£7,500 for a heat pump, or £9,000 when replacing oil or LPG.** The £9,000 rate runs until 31 March 2027, and a typical 3-bed semi at £11,000 to £15,500 comes down to £3,500 to £8,000.

**Owners in England and Wales replacing fossil fuel or electric heating.** The installer must be MCS certified; landlords qualify, social housing and most new builds do not, and since 28 April 2026 you no longer need a valid EPC.
**Your MCS installer applies, not you.** Get three quotes, agree one, confirm your consent when Ofgem contacts you, then pay only the balance after the grant.

**It is a fixed sum off the quote for the whole job.** Recorded costs cover the system, labour and VAT; ask whether the cylinder and radiator upgrades are included, and budget separately for insulation.

sections.h2: Cost breakdown with the BUS grant
sections.answer: **£3,500 to £8,000 out of pocket for a 3-bed semi.** The whole job is £11,000 to £15,500 before the £7,500 grant, or £2,000 to £6,500 with the £9,000 oil or LPG grant.
**Cheaper than gas only on a heat pump tariff.** A 3-bed semi costs £705 a year on a 19.8p heat pump tariff against £877 for gas, but £937 on a standard tariff.
**Stack them where you qualify.** Eligible households can get ECO4 insulation until 31 December 2026, and 0% VAT until 31 March 2027 is worth about £550 to £780 on an £11,000 to £15,500 job.

**A correctly designed heat pump keeps the whole home at 21°C.** Most installs fall under permitted development, and the extra £1,500 for oil and LPG homes ends on 31 March 2027, so there is no advantage in waiting.

**Grant rules come from GOV.UK, the 2026 amendment regulations and Ofgem**, installed costs from the Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics for August 2026, efficiency from the Electrification of Heat trial and prices from the Ofgem price cap.
**A scheme where energy suppliers fund upgrades for low income homes.** Ofgem runs it in Great Britain, it puts insulation before heating, and it runs until 31 December 2026.

**Owners of homes rated D to G, or private tenants in E to G homes, where someone claims a qualifying benefit.** Social housing rated E to G qualifies on the property alone, and councils can refer households below £31,000.

**Insulation first, then heating, as a whole house package.** It covers loft, cavity and solid wall insulation, boilers, heating controls and, in some homes, heat pumps and solar panels; windows and doors are rarely funded.
**Up to £151 a year for a 3-bed semi.** Measured savings run from £20 for a condensing boiler to £151 for solid wall insulation, and several measures together do not simply add up.
**Through your council or a participating energy supplier, as there is no government form.** An assessor surveys the home, the installer does the work, and you should never pay an upfront fee.
**Yes, if the home is rated E, F or G and the tenant qualifies.** The tenant needs a qualifying benefit or a council referral, and the landlord must consent and may be asked to contribute.

sections.h2: ECO4 Flex: the council referral route
sections.answer: **Your council can refer you without a qualifying benefit.** The most common route is a gross household income below £31,000; the others are low income proxies, a health referral and council targeting.

sections.h2: Quality standards and what to expect
sections.answer: **All work must meet PAS 2035 and use TrustMark registered installers.** Quality still varies, so check that damp and ventilation are assessed, and take unresolved problems to TrustMark's dispute resolution service.
**There will be no ECO5.** ECO4 closes on 31 December 2026 and support moves to council run grants, so apply now: the work must be installed by then, not just approved.

**The Boiler Upgrade Scheme, 0% VAT and the Warm Home Discount are also available.** BUS gives £7,500 towards a heat pump, or £9,000 for oil or LPG homes until 31 March 2027, and the discount is £150.

sections.h2: Making the most of ECO4 improvements
sections.answer: **Get a new EPC, learn your heating controls and check your bills.** Cheap DIY extras such as draught-proofing and secondary glazing tackle the heat loss ECO4 did not cover.
**Eligibility comes from GOV.UK and the ECO4 Order 2022, and scheme rules from Ofgem.** Measures and savings come from DESNZ statistics, and costs from the Energy Saving Trust.

sections.h2: How much does solid wall insulation cost?
sections.answer: **About £12,000 inside or about £15,000 outside for a typical 3 bed semi.** A terrace costs less and a detached house more, and repairs needed before external work are extra.

sections.h2: Annual savings from solid wall insulation
sections.answer: **About £151 a year for a 3 bed semi on gas.** That comes from a measured 17.3% fall in gas use; savings run from £98 for a 2 bed flat to £201 for a 4 bed detached house.
**Over 50 years at full price.** With a £151 yearly saving, £12,000 or £15,000 of work does not pay back on bills alone, so check for ECO4 funding first, which can cover the entire cost.

sections.h2: Internal vs external: which should you choose?
sections.answer: **Internal is cheaper; external performs better.** Internal leaves the outside unchanged but takes room space, while external keeps room sizes and avoids cold spots but needs scaffolding and may need planning permission.

**Done well it works for decades; done badly, internal insulation can trap moisture.** Fix existing damp first, use materials that suit the wall, keep ventilation working and insist on a 25 year guarantee.

sections.h2: Grants and funding for solid wall insulation
sections.answer: **ECO4 can fund it for eligible households until 31 December 2026.** ECO4 Flex and council Warm Homes: Local Grants help some low income homes, and installation carries 0% VAT until 31 March 2027.

sections.h2: How solid wall insulation affects your EPC
sections.answer: **It is one of the most effective ways to improve an EPC rating.** For a home on the edge of a band it can be enough to move it up one, which matters most for landlords.

**Internal insulation goes in room by room; external needs scaffolding for the whole job.** Inside, fittings come off, go back on and rooms need redecorating; outside, boards are fixed, meshed and rendered.

sections.h2: Combining solid wall insulation with other upgrades
sections.answer: **Insulate first, then fit a smaller heat pump.** The usual order is loft insulation, solid wall insulation, draught-proofing, then a heat pump sized to the improved home, with solar panels on top.
**Savings come from DESNZ NEED Impact of Measures and costs from the Energy Saving Trust.** Energy prices come from the Ofgem price cap, heating oil from BoilerJuice and VAT from HMRC.

sections.h2: Heat pump tariffs open in September 2026
sections.answer: **They charge less in set hours of the day, and all need a smart meter.** Cosy Octopus is about 13p off-peak against the 26.32p standard cap rate, and rates vary by region.
**Cosy Octopus for most homes, EDF Heat Pump Tracker if you want no peak.** Cosy gives eight cheap hours in three windows with no exit fee, but its 4pm to 7pm peak costs extra.
**Cosy Octopus saves most, £232 (25%) a year on a 3-bed semi.** It costs £705 against £937 on the standard rate; the other tariffs save £109 to £178, and Agile with no controls saves only £7.
**OVO Heat Pump Plus closed and Cosy Octopus added a 12 month fix.** Electricity carries no VAT from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027, so compare tariffs on their October prices.

sections.h2: How to shift heating to off-peak
sections.answer: **Heat in the cheap windows and coast through the peak.** Warm the house from 4am, heat the cylinder in the afternoon window, and let a smart thermostat schedule it, which is the only sensible way on Agile.
**No exit fee on Cosy, EDF or E.ON, but standing charges vary.** EDF Heat Pump Tracker and E.ON Next Pumped charge 42.92p a day in London up to 67.66p in North Wales and Merseyside.
**Octopus, EDF and ScottishPower make you join a standard tariff first.** You move across once the smart meter connects, usually around 14 days, while E.ON Next lets you sign up directly.

sections.h2: Combining a heat pump tariff with solar panels
sections.answer: **Solar covers spring and summer days and the tariff covers winter.** The 1pm to 4pm windows on Cosy and EDF overlap the sunniest hours, and a battery lets you run the evening peak on stored power.

**Rates come from the suppliers' own pages and price feeds, checked on 25 September 2026.** Standard rates come from the Ofgem price cap and heat pump efficiency from the Electrification of Heat trial.
**£55 to £150, and £65 to £95 for a 2 or 3-bed terrace or semi.** Bigger, more complex homes take longer to survey and cost more, but the certificate is identical whoever you book.
**There is no regional price scale.** Assessors set their own fees and London prices sit inside the national range; size, remote rural travel and rush bookings are what add to the price.
**Most homes already have a certificate you can download free.** One lodged less than ten years ago is still valid, but it will not show improvements made since the visit.

sections.h2: What the assessor does on the visit
sections.answer: **An accredited assessor measures the home and records what they can see or be shown.** Under RdSAP 10 anything unevidenced gets a default that is usually worse, so find your paperwork before the visit.

sections.h2: When you need an EPC, and the £200 penalty
sections.answer: **You need one before marketing a home to sell or let.** Trading standards can charge £200 per breach; renewing a tenancy with the same tenant or improving your own home needs none.

**Only a few narrow cases are exempt.** They include some listed buildings, places of worship, temporary buildings, standalone buildings under 50 square metres, homes due for demolition and some holiday lets.

sections.h2: How to pay less, and what a free EPC really is
sections.answer: **Check the register first and book a local assessor directly.** An estate agent's free EPC is genuine but serves the marketing, and a £65 to £95 reassessment after improvement work is the cheapest part of the project.

sections.h2: Lifting the score before the assessor arrives
sections.answer: **Find your paperwork first: it costs £0.** Evidence of cavity insulation, the boiler model and loft depth avoids worse defaults, and topping the loft up to 270 mm adds about 7 points in our model.
**New certificates with four headline metrics are due in the second half of 2027, with no firm date yet.** Existing certificates keep their ten years, so one lodged today runs for ten years.
**Prices come from assessor and provider price lists checked in September 2026, as there is no official list.** Rules come from the 2012 regulations, the RdSAP 10 approval and GOV.UK guidance.

sections.h2: What a heat pump costs in a flat
sections.answer: **£11,500 to £12,200 at the median, or £4,000 to £4,700 after the £7,500 grant.** A 2 bed flat costs £455 a year to heat on a heat pump tariff, against £566 on gas and £605 on standard electricity.

**It is the biggest hurdle.** The outdoor unit needs freeholder or management company approval, so check your lease first, and in England permitted development covers only one air source heat pump per block of flats.

sections.h2: Where to put the outdoor unit
sections.answer: **On an external wall, a balcony or at ground level.** A wall must take about 100 kg for a small unit, a balcony needs clearance and a weight check, and a ground floor pad is simplest.

**Small units can stay inside the 37 dB limit**, even with the other flats counting as neighbours. Grant's 4 kW Aerona 290 works out at about 31 dB(A) three metres from a window; anti-vibration mounts are essential.

sections.h2: Alternatives if a heat pump is not possible
sections.answer: **An air-to-air heat pump, electric radiators or infrared panels.** Air-to-air units have had a £2,500 grant since April 2026 but do not heat water; the electric options need no outdoor unit but cost more to run.

sections.h2: Insulation matters even more in flats
sections.answer: **Insulate first.** On our model insulation moves the running cost more than flat size: a well insulated 2 bed flat costs £469 a year on standard electricity against £481 on gas.

**Costs come from the DESNZ Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics, August 2026.** Efficiency comes from the Electrification of Heat trial, prices from the Ofgem price cap and Cosy Octopus, and planning and noise rules from legislation.gov.uk and MCS 020(a).

sections.h2: Bills by EPC band, every band
sections.answer: **A typical band D home pays £1,834 a year, band C £1,591.** The spread is smaller than most people expect: a band F home pays about £763 a year more than a band B home.

sections.h2: Monthly cost by band at a glance
sections.answer: **From £124 a month in band B to £187 in band F**, with band D at £153 and band C at £133. These are medians, so half of homes in each band pay less.

sections.h2: Why band A is not the cheapest on the meter
sections.answer: **Around three in ten band A homes have no gas**, so more of their heating is billed at 26.32p per kWh for electricity, not 7.97p for gas. Treat bands A and G as indicative: both are small groups.

sections.h2: What the certificate says you should pay
sections.answer: **More than homes really pay, and the gap widens as the band worsens.** A band E home is modelled at £3,011 a year but pays £2,070; to heat E, F or G properly, budget from the modelled figure.

sections.h2: What moving up one band saves
sections.answer: **About £242 a year from D to C**, the biggest step, followed by E to D at £237. Loft and cavity wall insulation together can make the D to C jump for about £2,950, often less with a grant.
**Band C from 1 October 2030.** Every privately rented home must meet a band C equivalent standard, up from band E now, and a band E rental costs the tenant about £479 a year more than band C.
**It depends more on your tariff than your band.** A well insulated 3 bed semi on a heat pump tariff spends about £200 a year less on heating than on gas, and about the same on a standard tariff.

**Consumption comes from the DESNZ National Energy Efficiency Data-Framework, 2024 meter readings.** Modelled costs come from the DESNZ fuel poverty tables, band boundaries from BRE SAP 10.2 and prices from the Ofgem price cap.

sections.h2: Every UK energy grant and whether it is open today
sections.answer: **Most are open; the Great British Insulation Scheme and HUG2 have closed.** The £7,500 Boiler Upgrade Scheme is funded to 2030, ECO4 closes on 31 December 2026 and 0% VAT ends on 31 March 2027.

sections.h2: The four things that decide your answer
sections.answer: **Your nation, benefits or income, EPC band and whether you own the home.** Nation rules out the most people: the Boiler Upgrade Scheme is England and Wales only, and the Warm Homes: Local Grant England only.

**£7,500 for a heat pump under the Boiler Upgrade Scheme**, or £9,000 for off grid oil or LPG homes until 31 March 2027. If you qualify for ECO4, chase it first: measures must be installed by 31 December 2026.

**The Warm Homes Plan, worth £15 billion.** For a low income household in England, the practical route after ECO4 closes is the Warm Homes: Local Grant through the council; a single low income scheme is planned from 2027/28.
**It is a model, not a reading of your bills.** An assessor records the home and the government's SAP model turns its modelled running cost per square metre into a score from 1 to 100, banded A to G.

sections.h2: How to improve your EPC rating in 2026
sections.answer: **Start with what your home lacks.** With under 100mm in the loft, insulating it costs about £750 for about 7 points; with good insulation and an old gas boiler, a heat pump adds about 12.

**Cheapest per point: LED lighting and smart controls.** Loft insulation in a bare loft costs about £750 for about 7 points, cavity walls about £2,200 for about 8, and solid wall insulation is the dearest per point.
**Band E today, a new standard from 1 October 2030.** The maximum fine then rises to £30,000 per property per breach, and landlords must spend up to £10,000 per property on qualifying improvements.

sections.h2: What the 37 dB(A) limit means in practice
sections.answer: **It sets how far the unit must be from a neighbour's window.** A 60 dB(A) unit on the ground against one wall needs 8.0 m, or 2.5 m if a solid wall hides the window.

**The MCS 020(a) calculation must give 37.0 dB(A) or less 1 metre outside a neighbour's habitable room window or door.** If it fails, the unit is not permitted development and needs planning permission.
**The model, how hard it works, where it sits and vibration.** Hard surfaces and corners raise the level, and more than three reflecting surfaces fails the calculation outright.

sections.h2: How to reduce heat pump noise
sections.answer: **Choose a quieter unit, add distance, fit anti-vibration mounts and use a solid barrier.** Each doubling of distance cuts about 6 dB, and a qualifying wall or fence counts as 10 dB.
**Talk to neighbours early and show them the MCS 020(a) result for their window.** Even a compliant unit can be investigated by the council as a statutory nuisance.
**Most sound comes from the outdoor unit.** Indoors you may hear a circulating pump, or a hum if the unit is fixed without anti-vibration mounts.
**A heat pump is loudest in cold weather, when it is also least efficient.** In the Electrification of Heat trial the median unit fell from 3.37 at 10°C to 2.37 at minus 3°C, so insulate first.
**MCS standards, planning law and trial data.** MCS 020(a), MCS noise guidance, legislation.gov.uk, GOV.UK and the Electrification of Heat trial, all checked on 25 September 2026.

sections.h2: Cost and savings by battery size
sections.answer: **A 5 kWh battery costs around £4,600 and adds about £180 a year on a 4 kW system.** Bigger batteries add little more: 10 kWh gives £218, as there is rarely enough surplus to fill them.
**Only by the gap between buying and exporting.** Each stored kWh saves 26.32p minus your export rate, about 14p on a 12p tariff, so a 5 kWh battery is worth about £180 a year.

sections.h2: Payback: solar only vs solar plus battery
sections.answer: **A battery roughly doubles payback on a flat rate tariff.** A 4 kW system alone pays back in 10.7 years, and in 20.6 years with a 5 kWh battery, counting one £4,600 replacement.

sections.h2: When a battery is worth it

sections.h2: Making your existing insulation last longer

sections.title: Where do draughts come from?
sections.answer: **Mostly through suspended timber floors, windows, external doors and unused chimneys.** Letterboxes, loft hatches, skirting gaps and pipe holes add more; older homes with sash windows and timber floors usually leak the most.

sections.title: How do you draught-proof each area?
sections.answer: **Seal the accidental gaps with strips, brushes, filler and excluders, and leave the vents alone.** Use foam or rubber strip on casements, brush pile on sashes, flexible filler on floorboards and a removable excluder in an unused chimney.

sections.title: Should you do it yourself or hire a professional?
sections.answer: **About £250 for a professional to do the windows and doors of a whole house, and less if you do it yourself.** A chimney pot cap starts from around £150; sash windows and period features may need a professional.

sections.title: How much does draught-proofing save?
sections.answer: **About £55 a year, paying back in about five years at the professional price and sooner if DIY.** An unused open chimney saves about £45 more, and turning the thermostat down from 22°C to 21°C saves about £120.

sections.title: Should you draught-proof before a heat pump?
sections.answer: **Yes, draught-proof first.** A heat pump delivers warmth at lower temperatures, so draughts are more noticeable; with loft and cavity insulation, it cuts heat demand and can allow a smaller, cheaper heat pump.

sections.title: How do you keep a draught-proofed home ventilated?
sections.answer: **Seal the gaps but keep the ventilation working.** Keep trickle vents open, extractor fans working and air bricks clear; a home with no trickle vents, wall vents or mechanical ventilation may already be too airtight.

sections.title: How do you insulate a suspended timber floor?

sections.title: How do you insulate a solid concrete floor?

sections.h2: Underfloor ventilation: do not block it

sections.title: What causes condensation, and how do you fix it?
sections.answer: **Cold surfaces, too much moisture and too little heating.** Fix ventilation first as it is cheapest and fastest, then insulate, then heat the rooms you use to at least 18°C.

sections.title: How do you fix it room by room?
sections.answer: **Run extractor fans in the bathroom and kitchen, and open bedroom vents or a window each morning.** Pull furniture away from external walls, and rule out leaks and other damp before blaming condensation.

sections.title: How can you tell it is not condensation?
sections.answer: **Damp that is worse in wet weather, or on walls that are not external, may be rising or penetrating damp.** A qualified damp surveyor can diagnose it, and tenants should report damp and mould to their landlord in writing.

sections.title: Does insulation make condensation worse?
sections.answer: **No, as long as you keep ventilating.** Insulation raises inside surface temperatures, which cuts condensation; it only goes wrong when a tightly sealed home gives the moisture nowhere to go.

sections.h2: Why your bill might be higher than average
sections.title: Why might your bill be higher than average?
sections.answer: **Usually poor insulation, an old boiler, a high thermostat or a standard variable tariff.** A poorly insulated 3 bed semi uses around 31% more gas than a well-insulated one: £1,081 against £854.

sections.h2: Average gas consumption by property type
sections.title: How much gas does a home use?
sections.answer: **From 5,600 kWh a year in a 1 bed flat to 19,500 kWh in a 5 bed detached house.** An average 3 bed semi uses 11,000 kWh, costing £985 a year.

sections.h2: Average electricity use by number of bedrooms
sections.title: How much electricity does a home use?
sections.answer: **From 1,666 kWh a year with one bedroom to 4,581 kWh with five or more, costing £639 to £1,406.** A 3 bedroom home uses 2,659 kWh, about £900; an electric car or heat pump adds more.

sections.h2: How to reduce your energy bills
sections.title: How can you cut your energy bill?
sections.answer: **Insulate first, then check your tariff, turn the thermostat down and consider a heat pump or solar.** Homes that had cavity wall insulation used a median 12.0% less gas, and many get it free through ECO4.
**Energy prices come from the Ofgem price cap for October to December 2026.** Consumption comes from our heat demand model fitted to DESNZ NEED data, and heating oil prices from BoilerJuice.

sections.h2: Energy bills by number of occupants
sections.title: What does each household size pay?
sections.answer: **£1,496 a year for one adult, £1,888 for two and £2,289 for four.** The cost per adult falls as the household grows, because heating is largely fixed by the size of the home.

sections.title: How much does property type matter?
sections.answer: **More than household size: from £1,126 a year for a well-insulated 1-bed flat to £2,835 for a 5-bed detached house.** The same homes at band E pay roughly 24 to 28% more for gas.

sections.title: What drives the differences?
sections.answer: **Heating, which depends on the home's heat loss rather than how many people live there.** Hot water and electricity for appliances and lighting are what rise with each extra person.

sections.title: How can you cut your bill?
sections.answer: **For a 3-bed semi on gas, cavity wall insulation saves about £105 a year and loft insulation about £28.** With a heat pump, a heat pump tariff saves about £232, and DIY draught-proofing costs under £250.

**Consumption by number of adults comes from the DESNZ NEED consumption tables 2026, and prices from the Ofgem price cap.** Measured insulation savings also come from DESNZ NEED, and insulation costs from the Energy Saving Trust.

sections.h2: Why the difference is so large
sections.title: Why is the difference so large?
sections.answer: **An electric boiler turns 1 kWh of electricity into 1 kWh of heat, while the median heat pump in the trial gave 2.78.** So heat costs 8.6p to 10.3p a unit from a heat pump, against 26.32p from an electric boiler.

sections.title: How much cheaper is a heat pump to run?
sections.answer: **£2,606 a year with an electric boiler in a 3-bed semi, against £705 with a heat pump on a heat pump tariff.** Even on a standard tariff, the heat pump saves £1,062 to £2,214 a year in the four example homes.

sections.title: What does each cost to install?
sections.answer: **£11,000 to £15,500 for a heat pump, or £3,500 to £8,000 after the grant; an electric boiler costs much less.** Saving £1,901 a year in a 3-bed semi on a heat pump tariff, the heat pump pays back in about 2 to 4 years.

sections.h2: When an electric boiler still makes sense
sections.title: When does an electric boiler still make sense?
sections.answer: **In small flats with no outdoor space, homes with very low heat demand, on a tight budget or before a move.** In a well-insulated 1-bed flat the saving is about £630 a year, so payback takes about 4 to 10 years.

sections.title: What does the switch involve?
sections.answer: **An outdoor unit, a hot water cylinder if you have none, larger radiators where needed and new controls.** Your MCS certified installer removes the old boiler and handles the Boiler Upgrade Scheme application.

sections.title: Do solar panels help?
sections.answer: **Partly, mostly with hot water in spring and summer rather than winter heating.** The median home bought 12.2% less electricity in its first year with panels, while a heat pump cuts heating electricity by about two thirds.
**Running costs use the Ofgem price cap and efficiency comes from the Electrification of Heat trial**, with installed costs from DESNZ Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics and grant rules from GOV.UK.

sections.h2: Why heat pumps need different radiators
sections.title: Why do heat pumps need different radiators?
sections.answer: **A heat pump is most efficient making cool water, and radiators give out less heat at low temperatures.** In the trial, running at 55°C instead of 35°C used about 47% more electricity for the same heat.

sections.h2: How much bigger radiators need to be
sections.title: How much bigger do radiators need to be?
sections.answer: **Rated output of about 3.1 times the room's heat loss at 41 to 45°C, against 1.9 times at 51 to 55°C.** So a radiator rated 1,000 W gives only about 320 W at 41 to 45°C.

sections.h2: How to check your existing radiators
sections.title: How do you check your radiators?
sections.answer: **Divide each radiator's rated output by the factor for your planned flow temperature and compare it with the room's heat loss.** At 45°C a radiator rated at 1,000 watts gives about 320 watts; your MCS installer does this room by room.

sections.title: Which radiators usually need replacing?
sections.answer: **Small single-panel radiators in large rooms, bathroom towel rails, and small radiators in kitchens and hallways.** A radiator rated at 800 watts gives only about 260 watts with water at 45°C.

sections.title: Which radiators often survive?
sections.answer: **Large cast iron radiators, oversized modern ones, double convectors and radiators in well-insulated rooms.** Insulating first helps: in the MCS example, a room's heat loss fell from 1,671 W to 976 W and it then worked at 45°C.

sections.title: What can replace a radiator that is too small?
sections.answer: **A larger panel radiator in the same space, a fan-assisted radiator, or underfloor heating.** In the MCS example a same-size double convector gave about 70% more output; underfloor heating usually only suits a major renovation.

sections.title: What should your installer provide?
sections.answer: **A room by room heat loss calculation, each radiator's output at the planned flow temperature, and which need upgrading, with costs.** If an installer proposes a heat pump without one, that is a red flag.
**Radiator sizing comes from the MCS Heat Emitter Guide and efficiency by flow temperature from the Electrification of Heat trial**, with the grant rules from GOV.UK.

sections.title: How much cheaper is a heat pump to run?
sections.answer: **£1,752 a year for storage heaters in a 3-bed semi, against £705 for a heat pump on a heat pump tariff.** Across the four example homes, the heat pump tariff saves £666 to £1,389 a year.

sections.h2: Why storage heaters cost so much
sections.title: Why do storage heaters cost so much?
sections.answer: **They turn each unit of electricity into one unit of heat, while a heat pump gave 2.55 to 3.05.** Daytime top-up costs about 32p/kWh on Economy 7, and you set each night's charge by guessing tomorrow's weather.

sections.title: What does the switch involve?
sections.answer: **A heat pump plus radiators, pipework and a hot water cylinder if the home has none.** The heat pump costs £3,500 to £8,000 after the grant, with radiator and pipework work priced separately.

sections.title: When should you keep storage heaters?
sections.answer: **In a small, well-insulated flat with no outdoor space, or when you rent.** There, modern high heat retention storage heaters may be the practical choice, at £900 to £1,400 per room fitted.

**Standard rates come from the Ofgem price cap and Economy 7 rates from Octopus Energy's public price feed**, with efficiency from the Electrification of Heat trial and installed costs from DESNZ Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics.
